subject: Reading Comprehension
text: PASSAGE (SRC-02-P1): A vaccine works less like a medicine and more like a rehearsal. Instead of attacking an infection directly, it presents the body with a harmless version of a germ, or merely a fragment of one, so that the immune system can study it in advance. Certain white blood cells respond by producing antibodies shaped to fit that particular invader, while others, known as memory cells, keep a record of the encounter for years. If the real germ arrives later, the body recognises it quickly and mounts a defence before serious illness can take hold. This explains why a vaccine against one disease offers no help against another: the training is highly specific. It also explains why some vaccines need booster doses, since the memory of certain germs fades with time. The approach has limits. Germs that change their outer coat rapidly can slip past an old memory, which is why some vaccines must be updated regularly. Even so, the principle remains remarkably economical. By teaching the body to defend itself, a small dose given in advance can prevent suffering that no treatment afterwards could fully undo. || Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
option_A: The Human Body and Its Many Systems
option_C: Vaccines: Medicines That Attack Germs Directly

text: PASSAGE (SRC-02-P2): For many coastal towns, the first response to rising seas and stronger storms has been to build higher walls. A sea wall is visible, easy to explain and quick to approve, and it can protect a harbour or a busy road for decades. Yet engineers have learned that a wall often moves the problem rather than solving it. Waves that strike a hard barrier carry sand away from the beach in front of it, and neighbouring stretches of coast may erode faster than before. For this reason, a growing number of towns are combining walls with softer measures. Mangroves and salt marshes are replanted to absorb the force of waves, sand dunes are restored, and new houses are built on raised plinths or kept back from the shoreline altogether. Such measures are slower to show results and harder to defend at a public meeting, because their benefits appear only when a storm fails to cause the damage it once would have. They also require cooperation among fishermen, landowners and officials who may not share the same priorities. Adaptation, in the end, is less a single structure than a patient arrangement of many small decisions. || What is the central theme of the passage?

option_D: Sea walls are the only lasting answer to rising seas

text: PASSAGE (SRC-02-P2): For many coastal towns, the first response to rising seas and stronger storms has been to build higher walls. A sea wall is visible, easy to explain and quick to approve, and it can protect a harbour or a busy road for decades. Yet engineers have learned that a wall often moves the problem rather than solving it. Waves that strike a hard barrier carry sand away from the beach in front of it, and neighbouring stretches of coast may erode faster than before. For this reason, a growing number of towns are combining walls with softer measures. Mangroves and salt marshes are replanted to absorb the force of waves, sand dunes are restored, and new houses are built on raised plinths or kept back from the shoreline altogether. Such measures are slower to show results and harder to defend at a public meeting, because their benefits appear only when a storm fails to cause the damage it once would have. They also require cooperation among fishermen, landowners and officials who may not share the same priorities. Adaptation, in the end, is less a single structure than a patient arrangement of many small decisions. || Which of the following is the closest synonym of the word 'erode' as used in the passage?

subject: Reading Comprehension
text: PASSAGE (SRC-02-P3): Waiting is usually described as wasted time, the empty stretch between one useful activity and the next. A passenger on a delayed train checks the clock again and again, and every minute seems longer than the last. Yet the same minutes pass quite differently for a child waiting for a festival or a farmer waiting for the rains. What changes is not the length of time but our relation to it. When we cannot see an end, or feel that someone else controls it, waiting becomes a burden; when we know why we wait and trust that the wait will be rewarded, it can feel like part of the event itself. Several traditions have treated patience as a skill rather than a mere absence of action. To wait well is to remain attentive without being anxious, and to accept that some things ripen at their own pace. This does not mean that every delay deserves acceptance; a wait caused by carelessness should be corrected rather than admired. But a life spent treating every pause as an obstacle may miss what pauses offer: a moment to notice, to prepare and to reconsider. || According to the passage, waiting becomes a burden when:

option_B: we are waiting for a festival
option_C: we cannot see an end to it or feel that someone else controls it
option_D: we trust that the wait will be rewarded
